question: What is the difference between a data scientist and an ML engineer?
model_answer: A data scientist focuses on extracting insights, building and experimenting with models (exploration, feature engineering, prototyping). An ML engineer operationalises those models — they focus on production systems: scalable model serving, CI/CD for ML pipelines, monitoring for data drift, infrastructure, and latency/throughput optimisation. The ML engineer owns the model after the data scientist hands it off.
improvement_tip: Be specific about MLOps tools (MLflow, Kubeflow, SageMaker) to demonstrate production experience.

question: How would you design a real-time ML inference pipeline that handles 10,000 requests per second?
model_answer: Key components: (1) Model serving — TorchServe, TensorFlow Serving, or Triton Inference Server with batch inference; (2) API gateway — FastAPI/gRPC behind a load balancer; (3) Caching — Redis for repeated identical inputs; (4) Async queuing — Kafka for burst buffering; (5) Horizontal scaling — Kubernetes HPA on CPU/GPU utilisation; (6) Optimisation — ONNX export, TensorRT quantisation for GPU, model pruning; (7) Monitoring — Prometheus + Grafana for latency p95/p99.
improvement_tip: State specific latency targets (p99 < 50ms) and discuss trade-offs between throughput and latency.

question: What is model drift and how do you detect and handle it?
model_answer: Model drift occurs when production data distribution shifts from training data, degrading model performance. Two types: (1) Data drift — input feature distribution changes (e.g. user behaviour shifts); (2) Concept drift — relationship between input and target changes. Detection: monitor feature distributions (KS test, PSI), track prediction distribution, shadow mode testing. Handling: automated retraining triggers, champion-challenger deployment, regular data refresh.
improvement_tip: Mention tools like Evidently AI, Fiddler, or Arize for production drift monitoring.

question: Explain the difference between online learning and batch learning. When would you use each?
model_answer: Batch learning trains on a static dataset periodically (nightly, weekly). Pros: stable, reproducible, easy to validate. Cons: slow to adapt to data changes. Online learning updates the model incrementally with each new data point or mini-batch. Pros: adapts in real-time, no retraining overhead. Cons: sensitive to noisy data, catastrophic forgetting risk. Use batch for stable domains (medical imaging). Use online for dynamic data (stock prices, fraud, recommendation systems).
improvement_tip: Mention Vowpal Wabbit or River (scikit-multiflow) as online learning frameworks.

question: What is feature store and why is it important in ML systems?
model_answer: A feature store is a centralised repository for storing, sharing, and serving ML features consistently between training and serving pipelines. It solves: (1) Training-serving skew — the same feature computation is used in both; (2) Feature reuse — teams share features across models; (3) Point-in-time correctness — no data leakage using time-travel queries; (4) Operational efficiency — pre-computed features reduce online latency. Popular feature stores: Feast, Tecton, Hopsworks, AWS SageMaker Feature Store.
improvement_tip: Describe a scenario where training-serving skew caused a model to underperform in production.

question: Tell me about a time you improved model performance in production.
model_answer: STAR: Situation — recommendation model AUC degraded from 0.87 to 0.79 over 3 months. Task — diagnose and restore performance. Action — added data drift monitoring (PSI > 0.2 alert), traced drift to new product categories not in training data, added category embeddings, retrained with 6-month rolling window, deployed with A/B test. Result — AUC restored to 0.88, CTR improved 12%. Lesson: proactive monitoring beats reactive firefighting.
improvement_tip: Always link model metrics back to business metrics (CTR, revenue, churn).

question: How do you reduce model inference latency for a deep learning model in production?
model_answer: Strategies: (1) Model compression — pruning (remove low-weight parameters), quantisation (FP32 → INT8 with TensorRT), knowledge distillation (train small student from large teacher); (2) Runtime optimisation — ONNX export, TensorRT, OpenVINO, TorchScript JIT compilation; (3) Batching — dynamic batching on the serving layer; (4) Hardware — GPU inference for batch, custom ASIC for edge; (5) Caching — cache embeddings for repeated inputs; (6) Async/parallel — asynchronous pre/post-processing.
improvement_tip: Quote actual speedups — e.g., INT8 quantisation typically gives 2–4× speed-up with <1% accuracy drop.

question: How do you stay current with the rapidly evolving ML/AI landscape?
model_answer: Structured approach: (1) Papers — arXiv (cs.LG, cs.AI), Papers With Code for SOTA tracking; (2) Communities — Hugging Face forums, ML Twitter/X, fast.ai; (3) Courses — regularly audit Coursera/DeepLearning.AI new content; (4) Implementation — reproduce 1 paper per month to build intuition; (5) Internal sharing — host team paper-reading sessions; (6) Conferences — NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR proceedings.
